paper.title: GPT-4V(ision) is a Generalist Web Agent, if Grounded

evidence.quote: We take the screenshot image i i as the visual context without utilizing the HTML document h h for action generation.
evidence.support_explanation: Screenshot/task/history are visible for free-form intention generation; HTML is withheld at this stage.

evidence.quote: Alternatively, we provide the model with textual representations of elements as choices to facilitate grounding, which has already been proven effective in MindAct ( Deng et al., 2023 ) .
evidence.support_explanation: Ranked DOM-choice grounding is explicitly inherited from MindAct.

evidence.quote: we first employ the DeBERTa-base cross-encoder from MindAct ( Deng et al., 2023 ) to rank the top 50 elements for better comparison with its text-only counterparts. Then, we cluster elements into groups of 17 17 options for inference.
evidence.support_explanation: Same DeBERTa-base top50 ranker with groups of17; group size differs from MindAct.

evidence.quote: Here we approximate the oracle grounding method by asking human annotators to identify the model’s intended actions.
evidence.support_explanation: Oracle grounding is human annotation, not an autonomous component.

evidence.quote: The Cross-Domain setting assesses agent performance on tasks in two top-level domains held out from the training data.
evidence.support_explanation: Structural task/site/domain splits exist; construction-time independence of all development choices is a separate question.

evidence.quote: We align each HTML document in the dataset with its corresponding webpage screenshot image from the Mind2Web raw dump, which undergoes human verification to confirm element visibility and correct rendering for action prediction.
evidence.support_explanation: Screenshots are aligned to HTML and human-verified for visibility/rendering.
Full offline split task denominators, not the oracle or live subset.

evidence.quote: Step Success Rate (Step SR) measures the success of each action step. A step is successful only if the selected element and the predicted operation are correct. We report macro averages across tasks for these step-wise metrics.
evidence.support_explanation: Offline Step SR is reference element+operation agreement and macro-averaged by task; not exploration-enabled task success.

evidence.quote:
We develop a new online evaluation tool using Playwright 3 3 3 https://playwright.dev/ to evaluate web agents on live websites (instead of cached websites in offline evaluation). Our tool can efficiently tunnel multimodal inputs from the browser to the agent and convert the predicted action ( e , o , v ) (e,o,v) into a browser event for execution.
To adhere to ethical standards, our experiments are restricted to non-login tasks in compliance with user agreements, and we closely monitor agent activities during online evaluation to prevent any actions that have potentially harmful impacts, like placing an order or modifying the user profile.
evidence.support_explanation: Live browser execution exists with ethical restrictions and human monitoring.

evidence.quote:
In online evaluation, we pair a web agent with a human annotator, where the human was tasked to monitor agent actions that may change real-world states and determine whether each task was successfully completed. For comparative analysis, we include success rates from offline evaluation, denoted as Offline 0 (allowing zero wrong action) and Offline 1 (allowing one wrong action).
For a fair comparison between offline and online evaluations, we only re-write time-sensitive tasks to ensure they are still valid when the evaluation is conducted. For instance, we update the dates for flight-related tasks. Finally, we conduct the online evaluation on the same subset of total 90 90 tasks from the three test splits. For tasks invalidated due to website change, we resample from the corresponding test split.
evidence.support_explanation: 90 live tasks, human success judgment, date rewrites and replacement of invalid tasks.

evidence.quote: Figure 3: Whole task success rate across task difficulty levels. We categorize tasks based on the number of actions to complete, i.e., Easy: 1 1 - 4 4 , Medium: 5 5 - 9 9 , and Hard: 10 10 - 18 18 , with 37 37 , 35 35 , and 18 18 tasks in each group, respectively.
evidence.support_explanation: Difficulty thresholds and group denominators are readable, but chart values are not in supplied figure assets.

evidence.quote:
Online Success Rate by Task Difficulty. We investigate the performance of web agents on tasks across different difficulty levels. We estimate the task difficulty based on the number of actions taken by annotators during action trace annotation.
As shown in Figure 3 , the whole task success rate is negatively correlated with the number of actions—it decreases as the number of actions increases across all four methods. SeeAct Oracle consistently outperforms other methods across all difficulty levels.
Interestingly, the gap between SeeAct Oracle and SeeAct Choice enlarges on longer-horizon tasks.
This is understandable because grounding errors cascade to later steps; nonetheless, it further shows the challenge of grounding for GPT-4V and the need for better grounding methods.
evidence.support_explanation: Prose supports decreasing success with horizon, not exact subgroup percentages.

evidence.quote: To analyze the reasons behind the failures, we randomly sample 100 100 action predictions with correct action generation but wrong grounding results.
evidence.support_explanation: Grounding error audit is conditional on correct generation and incorrect grounding.

evidence.quote: Our analysis reveals that 54 54 % of the errors can be attributed to GPT-4V ’s tendency of visual illusion
evidence.support_explanation: Conditional100-error split:54% hallucinated mark and46% wrong association; not all-task error frequencies.

evidence.quote: We develop an online evaluation tool using Playwright to load webpages, acquire textual representation of interactive elements, and perform operations generated by web agents. We manually monitor each step of the model and assess whether it finishes the tasks. Attempts to log in, make final submissions, or perform other potentially harmful actions are prohibited to avoid negative consequences.
evidence.support_explanation: Human monitoring and prohibited actions restrict online autonomy and task scope.

evidence.quote: SeeAct Oracle . In the oracle setting, we manually implement the model’s intended actions. The action history is automatically generated by the model, with an added requirement to summarize actions in the "Element", "Operation", "Value" format in another turn conversation. To avoid overly long screenshots, we use screenshots of current views, and hence allow intentions of scrolling.
evidence.support_explanation: Oracle uses human implementation, extra summary turn and viewport scrolling; not a clean deployed grounder swap.

evidence.quote: SeeAct Choice . For a relatively fair comparison, we still adopt the ranker and top- 50 50 candidate setting, batching them into three option groups as described in offline experiments. We enable PRESS ENTER and TERMINATE for the model to make confirmation or stop the process.
evidence.support_explanation: Choice adds ENTER and TERMINATE, so action spaces are not fully fixed versus MindAct.

evidence.quote: During our tests, pop-up ads on webpages were manually closed.
evidence.support_explanation: Manual closing of advertisements is an intervention shared with browser trials.

evidence.quote:
| (Current Webpage Identification) Firstly, think about what the current webpage is.
 | (Previous Action Analysis) Secondly, combined with the screenshot, analyze each step of the previous action history and their intention one by one. Particularly, pay more attention to the last step, which may be more related to what you should do now as the next step.
 | (Screenshot Details Analysis) Closely examine the screenshot to check the status of every part of the webpage to understand what you can operate with and what has been set or completed. You should closely examine the screenshot details to see what steps have been completed by previous actions even though you are given the textual previous actions. Because the textual history may not clearly and sufficiently record some effects of previous actions, you should closely evaluate the status of every part of the webpage to understand what you have done.
 | (Next Action Based on Webpage and Analysis) Then, based on your analysis, in conjunction with human web browsing habits and the logic of web design, decide on the following action. And clearly outline which element in the webpage users will operate with as the first next target element, its detailed location, and the corresponding operation.
 | To be successful, it is important to follow the following rules: 1. You should only issue a valid action given the current observation. 2. You should only issue one action at a time.
evidence.support_explanation: Explicit static page/history/status/one-action reasoning prompt; no learned persistent improvement.

evidence.quote:
Referring Description | (Reiteration) First, reiterate your next target element, its detailed location, and the corresponding operation.
 | (Multichoice Question) Below is a multi-choice question, where the choices are elements in the webpage. From the screenshot, find out where and what each one is on the webpage. Then, determine whether one matches your target element. Please examine the choices one by one. Choose the matching one. If multiple options match your answer, choose the most likely one by re-examining the screenshot, the choices, and your further reasoning.
 | If none of these elements match your target element, please select [None of the other options match the correct element]. A. [CHOICE A] B. [CHOICE B] …
Format Answer | (Final Answer) Finally, conclude your answer using the format below. Ensure your answer is strictly adhering to the format provided below. Please do not leave any explanation in your answers of the final standardized format part, and this final part should be clear and certain. The element choice, action, and value should be in three separate lines.
 | Format:
 | ELEMENT: The uppercase letter of your choice.
 | ACTION: Choose an action from {CLICK, TYPE, SELECT}.
evidence.support_explanation: Choice matching includes none and a structured action interface, not a correctness certificate.

evidence.quote: | (Verification with the Screenshot) Then, please closely re-examine the screenshot to find whether your target element is marked by a red bounding box and has a white number on a black background at the bottom left corner of the bounding box, which is positioned closely next to the bounding box. If yes, use that number for your final answer. If not, please do not make them up. If it is not marked, please output "NA" as your target element in the following final answer part.
evidence.support_explanation: Annotation prompt explicitly asks NA rather than fabricated labels; failures remain despite instruction.

evidence.quote: World Model (for Websites). GPT-4V exhibits the potential of a "world model" for websites. As shown in Appendix F , GPT-4V can predict the state transitions on a website (e.g., what would happen if I clicked this button). Based on its awareness of website state transitions, GPT-4V can conduct speculative planning involving a sequence of subsequent actions in the future to complete the given task.
evidence.support_explanation: World-model wording denotes qualitative speculative planning rather than an explicit trained transition simulator.

evidence.quote: Error Correction Awareness. GPT-4V also exhibits the awareness of error correction in the previous actions. In the example in Appendix I , it realizes that the mobile phone number is invalid due to the wrong format and generates the description of the action to correct this error. This highlights the model’s potential for adaptation in online settings, where actions may not always follow pre-defined, ideal paths as in offline evaluations. This capability paves the way for adding robustness and reasonable dynamic planning.
evidence.support_explanation: Correction awareness is a qualitative example, not a recovery benchmark.

evidence.quote: After obtaining the top- k k candidates, we utilize the candidate set to prune the webpage snapshot and construct snippets that only include the selected candidates and their neighbours as inputs to an LLM.
evidence.support_explanation: Mind2Web/MindAct already performs top-k pruning and multiple-choice element selection; no novelty credit for inventing rank-then-choose.

signatures.operation: Compare heuristic attribute matching, ranked textual choices, visual labels, and human grounding.
signatures.output: Element ID plus CLICK/TYPE/SELECT and value; Playwright event
signatures.conditions: Candidate recall; DOM/screenshot alignment; parseable answer; human oracle not deployable
signatures.feedback: Offline reference match and live observed page
signatures.selection_rule: Choose among17-option groups including NONE; final candidate maps to DOM. Human identifies intended action for oracle.
signatures.selection_data: MindAct ranker; evaluation subset; markup development/test separation not established.
signatures.persistence: Fixed ranker/prompts/markup configuration, not adaptive retention.
signatures.claimed_effect: Choice beats other automatic grounding; oracle exposes residual grounding gap.
signatures.failure_boundary: Mark hallucination and label association; top50 misses; oracle is conditional upper-bound proxy.

signatures.information: Current real page and model history; human monitors safety and completion.
signatures.operation: Execute browser actions on90 tasks with date rewrites/resampling; compare offline all-reference-step score.
signatures.conditions: Non-login/non-harmful scope; manual pop-up closure; differing action interfaces
signatures.feedback: Actual page transitions and human task judgment
signatures.selection_rule: Resample invalid tasks within corresponding split, not automatic accepted model improvement.
signatures.persistence: Evaluation outcomes only; no method update retained.
signatures.later_use: Not applicable: no later-task training from trial results reported.
signatures.claimed_effect: Live exploration/path flexibility is missed by offline exact reference paths.
signatures.failure_boundary: Date/site drift, human intervention, no repeatability/common step-budget accounting.

gap.author_gap: Strong multimodal models can describe intended web actions but fail to ground them; text-only HTML agents miss visual semantics and offline all-path matching undervalues interaction.
gap.checked_gap: Same-GPT4V30-per-split experiments show automatic grounding32.7-42.0 stepSR for choices versus61.9-65.0 human-oracle. Real90-task choice success37.8 differs greatly from offline3.3. This supports a residual grounding/evaluation bottleneck, not unconstrained general autonomy.

lineage.relationship: Pre-existing DOM ranker, top-k pruning and multiple-choice element selection; explicitly borrowed.

gap.closest_adjacent: MindAct with the same ranker; marked-image grounding as an alternative; oracle as diagnosis rather than competitor.
gap.residue: Screenshot-only intent generation before DOM grounding, cleaned multimodal alignment and live-vs-static evaluation, with automatic grounding still substantially below privileged oracle.
gap.stakes: Wrong elements cascade over long tasks; cached-reference task metrics can reject valid alternate paths.
gap.method_response: Expose generation and grounding as separate observable stages; compare automatic grounding and approximate oracle; execute on live pages.
gap.remaining_gap: Autonomous grounding, fair action/compute budgets, repeatability, robust refusal, unassisted safety and construction-heldout online validation.
unresolved: Not an exhaustive historical novelty search.
Markup selection/dev-test separation and exact live evaluation date not reported in inspected protocol.

claims.text: Grounding is a major bottleneck for screenshot-derived GPT4V intent.
claims.baseline_control: Attributes/annotation/choices versus human oracle; same backbone, differing grounding inputs.
claims.selection_vs_test: Shared30-per-split subset; markup type chosen by ablation, development/test separation unspecified.
claims.denominator: 30 tasks per split; macro per-task step metrics, not90 online tasks per split.
claims.budget: Top50 candidates for choice/annotation, groups17; human oracle privileged.
counterevidence: Oracle correct interpretation is not a deployable solver; candidate/filter and generation changes not all factored.
claims.allowed_conclusion: Automatic grounding limits this tested configuration; no proof that grounding alone solves generalist web automation.

claims.text: SeeAct achieves better real-web whole-task success than text-only baselines.
claims.setting: Live public web,90 tasks, non-login and prohibited consequential actions.
claims.selection_vs_test: Date rewrites/resampling preserve split provenance; no independent development lock disclosed.
claims.denominator: 90 tasks aggregate across three30-task splits; no subgroup transfer SR inferred.
claims.budget: Oracle manual execution/scrolling/extra summary; Choice ENTER/TERMINATE; manual pop-up removal; equal caps and cost not given.
counterevidence: Backbones/observations/action spaces differ; human-safety monitor is not unattended autonomy; no repeat trials.
claims.allowed_conclusion: Author-reported monitored live result on this restricted sample, not our replication or intervention-free general success.

claims.text: Long horizons worsen grounding, and GPT4V can sometimes plan or correct errors.
claims.setting: Difficulty37/35/18 tasks; conditional100 grounding errors; appendix cases.
claims.baseline_control: Four live methods by difficulty; no randomized recovery intervention.
claims.selection_vs_test: Illustrative case selection; conditional error sample.
counterevidence: Actual Figure3 numeric bars missing; illustrations cannot establish learned simulator fidelity or systematic recovery effect.
claims.allowed_conclusion: Text supports qualitative horizon trend and conditional error categories only.

assessment.strongest_supported_claim: Author-reported human-monitored live90-task results show37.8% choice-grounded success and51.1% with human oracle, alongside fixed-backbone offline evidence that grounding restricts GPT4V intentions. Live execution supports more than reference-step matching, but does not establish unassisted generalist sufficiency.
unresolved: Exact Figure3 subgroup numeric results remain unknown; supplied figure2_v7 is a methods diagram.
Construction-time isolation of live heldout sites from prompt/markup development is not established; choose online conservatively rather than promote to transfer from split names alone.
Common step caps, live evaluation dates, repeated runs, intervention counts and full cost are unavailable.
assessment.replication_status: author_report_only; no code or agent experiments run
assessment.retained_assessment: Not applicable to static prompted system; within-task action history is not retained cross-task improvement.
assessment.rubric_warning: Provisional independent seat assessment against fixed draft_uncalibrated v2.2; not frozen calibration or accepted final.

G.reason: Concrete grounded-intent versus executable-element bottleneck is important and empirically separated. Independent MindAct source confirms inherited rank/choose lineage; residue is screenshot-informed generation plus diagnostic and live/offline discrepancy, not invention of multiple choice.

M.reason: Reconstructable information split predicts a human-grounding upper bound and different automatic grounding performance. Alternatives are meaningful, but human oracle does not specify an autonomous solution, and ranker candidate recall/markup tuning remain prerequisites.

X.reason: Prompt templates, DOM-choice parsing, candidate budgets, action execution and human-intervention boundaries are documented. Static loop is operationally clear; common stopping budget and systematic recovery validation remain absent. No retained improver fabricated.

E.measurement.reason: Human-monitored live90-task task success plus explicit offline metric definitions are stronger than step accuracy alone. Choice37.8 and oracle51.1 are distinct; no independent judge agreement, intervention-free replay or executable success audit.

E.causality.reason: Same-generator offline grounding interventions support bottleneck attribution. Text-only backbones, grouping5vs17, human oracle, scrolling/ENTER differences and manual interventions prevent isolating all live gains to vision or decomposition.

E.holdout.reason: Named cross-task/site/domain splits and visibility-verified screenshots support benchmark generalization coverage. Online subset preserves split sampling, but development/markup-selection independence and base-model contamination are not established; live aggregate is not per-heldout-site transfer evidence.

E.statistics.reason: Known full split denominators,90 live tasks and conditional100-error audit; difficulty bins are disclosed. No repeat runs/intervals or unconditional failure census; Figure3 subgroup values unknown rather than reconstructed.
search_scope: Supplied16 image assets; Figure3 bars unavailable

E.cost.reason: Top50,17-option groups and approximate visual input tokens are reported, but no end-to-end per-task latency/API cost, human labor budget, equal step cap or failure-cost accounting. This is partial budget evidence, not zero-cost proof.
search_scope: Sections3.2-4.3; Table1 token statistics; AppendicesA-D including online details

reason: Full substantive text, prompts, tables and supplied appendix figures reviewed; missing Figure3 numbers are nonessential to the overall metric judgments and remain explicitly unknown. Original broad claim retained and scoped, not silently narrowed.
readable_rationale: A useful early decomposition and diagnostic of screenshot intent versus actual grounding, with unusually informative offline-versus-live comparison and a directly checked MindAct ancestor. The strongest evidence is for a monitored restricted browser system and a grounding bottleneck, not a solved autonomous generalist agent. Human oracle privileges, action-space differences, markup selection and missing repeat/budget details limit causal and transfer claims.
